authors.sig: A Cypriot Levite named an apostle in Acts and a companion of Paul on his journeys. The Epistle attributed to him argues that the Mosaic law has been superseded by the gospel, though most modern scholars doubt he wrote it.

Chosen by lot to replace Judas among the Twelve, according to Acts 1:15-26. No writing of his survives directly, but Clement of Alexandria cites sayings from his lost Traditions of Matthias. Those fragments say that admiration of present things begins knowledge, and that the world is a book revealing its author.

One of the Twelve Apostles, named in all four New Testament apostle lists. Many scholars identify him with Nathanael of John's Gospel, and tradition makes him a martyr. A "Brief Statement" under his name is not an apostolic writing, since it cites Anselm and the Magdeburg Centuriators.

Christian writer associated with Rome and author of The Shepherd of Hermas. The work offers visions and commandments on repentance after baptism. The Muratorian Canon names him a brother of Pope Pius I, though the date of the work is disputed.

authors.aff: Monk and abbot of Chrysopolis; former first secretary to Emperor Heraclius
authors.sig: Monk and abbot of Chrysopolis who opposed Monothelitism, the imperial teaching of a single will in Christ. He wrote the Questions to Thalassius and the Mystagogy, and his commentaries on Pseudo-Dionysius shaped later medieval theology and mysticism.
His seven genuine letters are among the earliest post-apostolic Christian writings, central to early ecclesiology, the role of the bishop, and opposition to Docetism.

Bishop of Smyrna in the second century and a disciple of John the Apostle, according to Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Jerome. He wrote a Letter to the Philippians, among the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament. It preserves Ignatius's letters.

Bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia and an Apostolic Father. He wrote a five-book Exposition of the Sayings of the Lord that survives only in fragments preserved by Irenaeus and Eusebius. Those fragments report that Mark recorded Peter's preaching and that Matthew wrote the sayings in Hebrew.

The earliest known Christian apologist; his single surviving fragment is an early written defense of Christianity addressed to the Roman emperor Hadrian and an early witness to the historicity of Jesus' miracles.

A Greek writer under Hadrian, around AD 135, whom Eusebius praises as a historian. He is credited with the first book written solely against heresy, a refutation of the twenty-four books of Exegetica by the Gnostic Basilides. Only a fragment survives, quoted by Eusebius.

Known only through a single writer who cites him, he is named as the source for Hadrian's permanent banishment from Jerusalem after the Bar Kokhba revolt. Later readers linked him to a dialogue, a link that scholars dispute.

Bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia under the emperor Marcus Aurelius. He wrote an Apology to the emperor and two books On Truth, but only fragments survive. Eusebius preserves the account of the Thundering Legion in which Christian soldiers prayed for rain and victory.

The fragments here preserve one of the earliest post-apostolic witnesses to church order, the succession of Roman bishops down to Eleutherius, and traditions about James the Just; the surrounding notes show how later scholars reconstructed him.

A Stoic philosopher from Sicily who converted to Christianity and led the Catechetical School of Alexandria from about 180. Clement of Alexandria, his pupil, called him the Sicilian bee. Only a short fragment of exegesis under his name survives, arguing against Hermogenes and the Marcionites.
The fragments here preserve his polemic against Marcionite divisions, especially his report that Apelles admitted one first principle while rejecting the prophecies as from an opposing spirit.

Bishop of Jerusalem from about 333 to 336, and a confessor who was mutilated in an early fourth-century persecution. A fragment printed under his name in PG 5 argues that matter cannot be an unbegotten principle beside God, since there cannot be two uncreated first principles.

Bishop in Asia Minor in the late second century, he wrote to Pope Victor I for the churches of Asia in defense of keeping Easter on the fourteenth of Nisan. His letter is the main surviving voice of the Quartodeciman dispute. The Acts of Saint Timothy is also attributed to him.

Bishop of Caesarea Maritima who presided over a synod that opposed the Quartodeciman practice in the paschal controversy. A synodal epistle on the Paschal question survives under the synod's name and fixes the paschal limit after the equinox.

His surviving fragments are early evidence that the church tested writings attributed to the apostles and rejected forgeries — notably the Docetic Gospel of Peter — while the letter to Caricus and Pontius shows Montanism condemned across Asia and Thrace.

A Greek ecclesiastical writer probably from Asia Minor. He wrote a defense of the Church against Montanus. The work is lost, but Eusebius cites it and Jerome praises it. It circulated reports of the suicides of Montanus and his prophetesses and exposed Themison and Alexander.

Against Heresies is the earliest large-scale refutation of gnosticism and a foundational witness to Scripture, apostolic tradition and episcopal succession as marks of the true church. Irenaeus is also the earliest surviving witness to regard all four canonical gospels as essential.

Bishop of Rome from about 189 until his death in 199, whose letters survive. Sources give him an African origin and a father named Felix, and they disagree on when his episcopate began. He was succeeded by Zephyrinus.

authors.aff: Christian philosopher and teacher in Rome
authors.sig: His second-century apologies and dialogue defend Christianity against pagan accusation and Jewish objection. From prophecy he argues that Christ is born of a virgin as Isaiah 7:14 foretold, that salvation requires doing Christ's works, not mere profession, that Abraham was justified by faith before circumcision and that the church is the new Israel.

authors.aff: Christian community in Rome, pupil ('hearer') of Justin Martyr
authors.sig: Assyrian apologist and pupil of Justin Martyr in Rome. After Justin's death he broke with the church and embraced Encratite asceticism. His Oration against the Greeks argues that Greek learning was borrowed from barbarian sources. He also held that Plato drew on Pherecydes through Pythagoras.

authors.aff: Christian philosopher of Athens, active under Marcus Aurelius and Commodus
authors.sig: Athenian philosopher and convert to Christianity who wrote a second-century apology in 176 or 177. His Embassy (Presbeia) for the Christians argues that the name Christian is hated unjustly and asks the emperors to protect them by law. On the Resurrection of the Dead also survives under his name.

His Three Books to Autolycus contain an early use of the term Trinity. Writing against the Jews and the Greeks, he argues at length that Greek poets and philosophers borrowed their truths from Moses and the Hebrew prophets.

Head of the catechetical school at Alexandria for about two decades. He wrote the Exhortation to the Greeks, The Tutor and Miscellanies. In them he sets Christian teaching beside Plato and the Stoics. He argued that without faith there is no understanding. He also combated Gnostic teachers such as the Valentinians and Basilides.

Bishop of Rome from about 199 until his death on 20 December 217. Hippolytus opposed him as a man without higher theological training, and Eusebius credits him with combating the Theodoti. No writings survive under his own name.

authors.aff: Presbyter of the church of Rome
authors.sig: His fragments are among the earliest Roman witnesses to the apostolic sees at Rome — he cites the 'trophies' of Peter on the Vatican and Ostian Road — and to early disputes over Montanist prophecy and heretical tampering with Scripture.

authors.aff: Embassy to Rome for Emmaus (Nicopolis), Palestine
authors.sig: Christian traveler and historian from Palestine who wrote the Chronographiai, a universal chronicle running from Creation to AD 221. He set biblical chronology beside Hellenistic dating systems. A letter on the history of Susanna survives under his name.

Bishop of Rome from about 218 until about 222 or 223. Hostile sources say he was a former slave and banker who was condemned to the mines of Sardinia. Some works argue that Ulpian killed him on 22 October 223 rather than Alexander Severus.

The works under this name are not by Urban but fragments and citations preserved around him; they matter chiefly for what early writers attributed to him on penance, church property, and the treatment of the fallen.
His extant writings are a polemic against the Montanists (Cataphrygians), arguing that their 'new prophecy' is false prophecy and defending the fixed character of Gospel doctrine.

Bishop of Rome from 230 to 235 and the first pope on record to resign. He resigned while exiled on Sardinia so a successor could be elected. A Roman synod under him confirmed the condemnation of Origen. A Greek treatise against the Montanists is attributed to him but is anonymous.

Bishop of Rome from 235 until his death in January 236. He succeeded Pontian, who had been deported to Sardinia. A letter under his name survives but is generally regarded as a forgery because its attack on Arius postdates him.
Bishop of Rome from 236 until he died a martyr at the start of the Decian persecution in 250. Canon-law collections attribute letters to him that are argued to be pseudo-Isidorian forgeries.

Bishop of Jerusalem and a pupil of Clement of Alexandria. He founded a library of Christian theological works at Jerusalem. He allowed Origen to speak in the churches. Arrested in the persecution of Decius, he died in prison.

Bishop of Laodicea in Syria, he was a mathematician and philosopher in Alexandria before his ordination. He wrote a treatise on the time of the Paschal celebration, with a nineteen-year cycle beginning in 276 and an equinox rule for fixing the new moon of the first month. Later computists such as Bede argued over this material.
Athanasius used Theognostus's statements on the Son's generation from the Father's substance as an orthodox witness against Arian readings of his Origenist language.

Priest of Alexandria who probably headed the catechetical school and was called 'Origen the Younger' for his preaching and exegesis. Only fragments survive of his twelve treatises or sermons, including one on Luke and an Easter sermon on Hosea.

authors.aff: Presbyter of Antioch; president of the faculty of rhetoric
authors.sig: Presbyter of Antioch and rhetorician who debated Paul of Samosata in public before a gathering of bishops and presbyters. Shorthand writers took down the exchange, and Malchion then wrote the council's letter condemning Paul to the bishops of Rome and Alexandria.

authors.aff: Presbyter at Rome; first antipope (217/218–235); banished to Sardinia in 235 alongside Bishop Pontianus
authors.sig: His works are mostly exegetical: commentaries and fragments on Daniel, Proverbs and Genesis, and a catena-commentary on the Psalms preserved under Eusebius of Caesarea's name. Polemic against the monarchian Noetus and apocalyptic treatises on Christ and Antichrist make him an early witness to Logos theology and chiliasm.

Bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus who studied under Origen at Caesarea. His Panegyric Oration to Origen is commonly regarded as a firsthand account of Origen's teaching method. His canonical letters are often cited among the earliest surviving pieces of Greek canon law.

Head of the catechetical school at Alexandria before he became bishop there in 248. Most of his letters survive only as excerpts that Eusebius preserved. The current note says they defend divine providence against the atomists and Epicurus. He argued against Sabellianism that the Son's generation produces a distinct person of the same nature.

His Apocriticus preserves verbatim excerpts of a pagan anti-Christian work, generally attributed to a redaction of Porphyry's lost Against the Christians (though Hierocles has also been proposed), making it a key monument for the pagan-Christian controversy of late antiquity.
The Acts of the Disputation with Manes long served as an essential source for Mani's life and early Manichaeism, and the text here disputes Manes on sin, Scripture, Christ, the Law, and creation.

Presbyter of Caesarea Maritima who gathered a large library of biblical manuscripts and taught Eusebius. He was imprisoned for two years during the Diocletianic persecution and died as a martyr in 309. An Exposition of the Chapters of the Acts of the Apostles is argued to be his own work.

Bishop of Thmuis in the Nile Delta, he was beheaded in 306 during the Diocletianic persecution. A letter he wrote from prison describes the tortures of the confessors at Alexandria, and Eusebius preserves part of it as an eyewitness account.

Bishop of Alexandria from about 282 or 283 until his death in 300. He is credited with aiding the suffering inhabitants during Diocletian's siege of the city. The Epistle to Lucian that survives under his name is a seventeenth-century forgery, probably by Jérôme Vignier (1606–61).

authors.aff: Catechetical School of Alexandria; Christian School of Caesarea
authors.sig: Taught at Alexandria and later founded the Christian School of Caesarea. The churches of Palestine and Arabia regarded him as an authority. His surviving works are mostly exegesis. They include commentaries on John and Matthew and homilies on Jeremiah.

authors.aff: Monastery on the Mount of Olives, Jerusalem; later Aquileia
authors.sig: Translator of Origen and Eusebius into Latin as Greek learning faded in the West. He also wrote the History of the Monks and a Commentary on the Apostles' Creed. His quarrel with Jerome over Origen's orthodoxy in the 390s produced an Apology against Saint Jerome.

He was the first systematic opponent of Origen, attacking Origen's doctrine of the resurrection body while remaining indebted to Alexandrian allegory and faithful to the literal tradition of Irenaeus.
His treatise is one of the earliest and best-informed accounts of the Manichaean system as it first spread into Egypt, exposing its lack of philosophical demonstration.

His canonical epistle on penance for those who lapsed under persecution shaped the church's treatment of apostasy under coercion, and his excommunication of Arius marks him as an early opponent of Arianism.
His surviving letters — the encyclical letter after the Alexandrian synod and the letter to Constantinople — are the earliest anti-Arian documents and prepared the ground for Nicaea.

authors.aff: Bishop of Antioch, deposed and exiled to Trajanopolis
authors.sig: Bishop of Antioch who was among the prominent opponents at the Council of Nicaea in 325. In On the Ventriloquist against Origen he argues that the apparition of Samuel to Saul was a demon repeating Samuel's prior prophecies. A synod at Antioch deposed him on charges of Sabellianism, and Constantine banished him to Thrace.

authors.aff: Bishop of Bostra in Arabia, c. 362–371
authors.sig: Bishop of Bostra in Arabia from about 362 to 371, he faced Julian's attempt to have him expelled. He wrote a refutation of Manichaeism arguing that God is not the author of sin and that nothing created is evil by nature. Its fourth book is lost.
The held work is a small set of Greek patristic fragments from a bishop of uncertain date, valuable chiefly for its anti-Arian polemic and exegetical treatment of sin and grace.
Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine from about 313/314 until his death on 30 May 339. His historical and apologetic works include the Ecclesiastical History, Chronicle and Preparation for the Gospel.

authors.aff: Taught Greek at Siena, Ferrara, and Rome
authors.sig: His translations of Aristotle were considered superior in accuracy and style to earlier versions, and he was a notable defender of Aristotelianism in fifteenth-century Italy.

Archbishop of Crete and hymnographer, best known for the Great Canon. His homilies and orations preach on the cross as Christ's glory and argue against the Jews and against Herod. He represented the Jerusalem Patriarchate at the Sixth Ecumenical Council.

The chief fourth-century opponent of Arianism, called the 'Father of Orthodoxy'. His writings argue that the Son is begotten, not made, and consubstantial with the Father, shaping Trinitarian doctrine.

Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia from 370 until his death in 379. He defended the Nicene faith against Arianism and Apollinarianism. His Longer Rules set out a communal monastic life centered on prayer and manual labor.

His Catechetical Lectures and Mystagogical Catecheses are an important surviving record of how fourth-century Jerusalem instructed catechumens before baptism and expounded the creed throughout Lent, and document the liturgy and sacramental teaching of his day.

Succeeded Athanasius as bishop of Alexandria in 373. Valens's prefect Palladius drove him from the city and installed the Arian Lucius. He took refuge in Rome with Pope Damasus I and returned in 378. His surviving work defends his succession and denounces Lucius in an encyclical to all churches.

Patriarch of Alexandria from about 381 until his death in 384. He succeeded his brother Peter II and was called Aktēmōn, 'the Destitute.' A question-and-answer text on communion and church discipline survives under his name.

authors.aff: Bishop of Laodicea in Syria from about 360
authors.sig: Bishop of Laodicea in Syria from about 360 whose teaching that the divine Logos replaced the rational soul in Christ was condemned at Constantinople in 381. Some dispute that he wrote his Metaphrase of the Psalms and Fragments on the Psalms.

authors.n: Isaac the Jewish Convert (Isaac ex Judaeo Christianus)
authors.aff: Jewish convert to Christianity in the Roman Empire
authors.sig: A Jewish convert to Christianity in the Roman Empire in the fourth century. He wrote the Liber fidei de sancta trinitate et de incarnatione Domini. It is a short treatise defending the full deity of the Son and Spirit.

Bishop of Tarsus, he taught the literal, historical reading of Scripture against Alexandrian allegory. His pupils included Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia. Later critics found anticipations of Nestorianism in his Christology. Most of his writings survive only as fragments, including fragments on Romans.

Bishop of Helenopolis in Bithynia from 400. He spent nine years among the Nitrian monks of Egypt. His Lausiac History records the lives and sayings of Egyptian and Eastern monks and teaches on prayer and the defeat of demons.

Archbishop of Constantinople from 380 to 381, he later withdrew to Arianzus. His orations and letters defend the full deity of the Spirit against Arians and Apollinarians, and he coined the maxim 'what is not assumed is not healed.'

A recent study (Duffy 2025) argues he is the 'unknown scholiast' on the disputed mystical-experience passage of the Ladder of Divine Ascent discussed by Rodionov, alongside Psellos and Photios; his works are preserved in PG 97.

Bishop of Maiuma, the port of Gaza. He was a hymnographer whose canons for Easter, Christmas and the Exaltation of the Cross entered the Byzantine liturgy. He wrote a prose commentary on the poems of Gregory of Nazianzus (PG 38) and hymns (PG 98).

authors.aff: Monk (name David) at the monastery of Agathos, Constantinople
authors.sig: A monk and disciple of Arethas of Caesarea, he wrote some fifty hagiographies and a commentary on the Psalms with a moral exhortation for every psalm. His tetrasticha on the poems of Gregory the Theologian survive, though some verses are interpolated.

authors.aff: Physician at the imperial court of Constantinople under Constantius II and Julian the Apostate
authors.sig: Court physician at Constantinople under Constantius II and Julian the Apostate. He was the younger brother of Gregory Nazianzen. A set of catechetical dialogues printed under his name answers astrologers, Arians, Origenists and traducianists. Gregory Nazianzen is said to confirm that he wrote them.

Bishop of Iconium whom Basil of Caesarea placed in that office early in 374. He was an ally of Basil and Gregory against Arianism and Macedonianism. He is remembered mainly for his synodal letter on the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and his surviving homilies and orations preach on Christ's two natures and the resurrection.

authors.aff: Teacher in the church school of Alexandria, approved by Bishop Athanasius
authors.sig: A fourth-century Alexandrian exegete. Mainly through commentary on the Psalms and on Paul, his works defend the Son's consubstantiality with the Father and the full deity of the Holy Spirit against Arians and Macedonians, and also against Manichaeans.

Praetor of Constantinople who was still an unbaptized catechumen when Theodosius I chose him as archbishop in 381. Two short pieces printed under his name in PG 39 are of doubtful attribution: an exposition on Saint Theodore touching fasting and almsgiving and an account of the archbishop.
His surviving homilies combine rhetorical skill with moral exhortation — on sin, almsgiving, marriage, and judgment — and attack pagan customs such as the New Year feast (Adversus Kalendarum Festum).

His De natura hominis is the first known Christian compendium of theological anthropology, integrating Aristotle, Galen, Plato, and Stoic material into a Christian account of soul, body, free will, and providence; it shaped later Byzantine, Arabic, and Latin thought, and chapters on the soul circulated under Gregory of Nyssa's name.

Egyptian monk who became hegumen at Tabenna after Theodore the Sanctified died. Gennadius says he wrote a book on monastic discipline that explained nearly all of Scripture and that he gave his brothers as a testament before he died. The Latin Doctrina de institutione monachorum is traditionally held to be Jerome's translation of it.

Bishop of Thmuis in the Nile delta and an ally of Athanasius against Arianism. He wrote a polemic against the Manichaeans arguing that sin is an act of the will and not a substance, and that the body is not evil in its nature.

authors.aff: Founder of the cenobitic monastery at Tabennisi, Egypt
authors.sig: Founder of the cenobitic monastery at Tabennisi in Egypt, he organized monks into communities under a common rule. The earliest extant monastic rule is attributed to him. Works about him argue from Scripture that shared life points to the future restoration and that members should bear one another's burdens.

Egyptian monk from the village of Coma who withdrew into the desert around 270. He was among the first known to go deep into the wilderness and became the figure most associated with the Desert Fathers. A work attributed to him treats sanctification, sin and prayer.
The Asceticon was influential in the development of Eastern Christian asceticism and spirituality, treating sin, watchfulness of the heart, prayer, and the virtues for monks and solitaries.

authors.aff: Monk of Nitria and Kellia, Egypt
authors.sig: Ascetic who lived at Nitria and Kellia in Egypt and copied manuscripts there. His practical chapters treat the passions of acedia, vainglory and pride. Later councils condemned him with Origen. Yet his ascetical works circulated in Greek, Syriac and Latin.

A Christian Greek epic poet of Panopolis in the Egyptian Thebaid, dated by scholars to the late 4th and mid-5th centuries. He wrote the 48-book Dionysiaca, an epic on Dionysus in hexameters. He also wrote the Metabole, a paraphrase of John's Gospel in the same Homeric meter.
His works are mainly polemics against Eunomius defending the Son's coeternity and consubstantiality, with exegetical and ascetical treatises on the soul, creation and perfection in virtue.

Archbishop of Constantinople and a Greek Father whose homilies on Genesis, Matthew and John press each passage toward conduct. His teaching that love of money is the root of evils angered the wealthy. He also wrote against Jews, Arians and pagans.

Bishop of Gabala in Syria and a popular Antiochene preacher in Constantinople around 400. His homilies on the Baptism of Christ argue that Christ sanctifies the baptismal waters rather than being sanctified by them, and that the Trinity was manifested at his baptism.
Innocent I significantly advanced the doctrine of universal papal primacy through his influential decretals and his decisive intervention in the Pelagian controversy.

The work here preserves his paschal epistles and related fragments — including the claim that he compiled a 418-year paschal cycle — alongside material on Sunday as both first and eighth day, the restoration of lapsed clergy, and arguments against Origen.

A layman of the Eunomian party who lived in Constantinople and wrote a twelve-book Church History of the Arian controversy. The work survives through an epitome and scattered borrowings, and it preserves the Eunomian side of a dispute that Nicene historians suppressed.

Archbishop of Constantinople from 406 to 425, who had helped accuse John Chrysostom at the Synod of the Oak. After Chrysostom's death he restored his name to the diptychs and won communion with Rome from Innocent I.

Archbishop of Constantinople from 434 until his death in 446. He preached before Nestorius in 429 in defense of the title given to Mary. Orations, homilies and letters survive under his name, including a Letter on the Faith.

Archbishop of Constantinople from 446 to 449, he presided over a synod that condemned an archimandrite for denying two natures in Christ. His letters on the controversy and a christological defense survive under his name. Dioscorus had him deposed at the Robber Synod of Ephesus, and the Council of Chalcedon vindicated him in 451.

authors.aff: Superior of a laura at Ancyra, later hermit in Palestine
authors.sig: His ascetic treatises address sin, grace, baptism and unceasing prayer. They teach that confessing a shortcoming beats proud error and that contrition comes in saving and harmful kinds. He argues against those who think they are justified by works. Some scholars read him as anticipating Reformation theology on grace.

Bishop of Photice and an ascetic writer whose works entered the Philokalia. He signed the bishops' reply to Emperor Leo I's 457 encyclical affirming Chalcedon. Homilies under his name survive against the Arians and on the Ascension.

authors.aff: Deacon of the church of Gaza
authors.sig: Deacon of the church at Gaza and a strong ally of Bishop Porphyrius in closing the pagan temples there. He had entered Porphyrius's service around 395 during one of the bishop's visits to Jerusalem. His Life of Saint Porphyry survives in Greek and Latin and Georgian and narrates the destruction of the temple of Marnas.

The chief exegete of the Antiochene school. His commentaries on the Minor Prophets and the New Testament treat sin, providence and Christology through conditional prophecy and literal reading, against Apollinarius, Julian and Jewish interpretation.

A Neoplatonist bishop in Cyrenaica who studied under Hypatia at Alexandria. His Letters and Book on Providence treat providence and kingship in Attic prose that cites Homer and Plato more often than any Christian authority.

authors.aff: Circle of Empress Julia Domna in Rome; later settled in Tyre
authors.sig: A Greek sophist of the Roman imperial period who taught at Athens and joined the circle of Empress Julia Domna in Rome. He is not a church writer, and attribution of some pieces to him is disputed. His works include the Life of Apollonius of Tyana and the Lives of the Sophists.

Tutor to the sons of Emperor Theodosius I before he withdrew to the desert of Egypt. Sayings under his name survive in the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, with short exhortations on sin, mercy toward the neighbor, and doing good to all without distinction.

Their histories are indispensable documentary sources for fourth- and early fifth-century Christianity, especially the Arian controversy, and supplied much of the medieval Latin West's knowledge of that period through Cassiodorus's translation.

His Ecclesiastical History is one of the primary and most reliable sources for fourth- and early fifth-century church history, particularly for the Arian controversy and the early ecumenical councils.
One of the essential primary continuators of Eusebius's ecclesiastical history for the fourth and fifth centuries.

Patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444 and a central opponent of Nestorius. In Against Nestorius and the Explanation of the Twelve Chapters he argued that one Christ is God and man and that the Word suffered in the flesh. His treatise That the Virgin is Theotokos argues that Mary is truly Theotokos.

authors.aff: Monastery on Mount Pelusium, Egypt; monastery by the Jordan River
authors.sig: Priest and head of a monastery on Mount Pelusium in Egypt, chosen by his fellow monks. His letters of moral and exegetical counsel went to monks, bishops, and emperors. About 2,090 of his roughly 10,000 letters survive. A monk by the Jordan River met Saint Mary of Egypt and buried her.

authors.aff: Monk and abbot at Mount Sinai
authors.sig: A disciple of John Chrysostom who held high civil office in Constantinople before going to Mount Sinai. He lived some forty years there as a monk and abbot and wrote ascetical works. His Four Books of Letters, Treatise on Voluntary Poverty and On the Eight Evil Thoughts teach on sin and prayer.

Bishop of Cyrrhus from about 423 and a defender of the Antiochene side against Cyril of Alexandria. His Philotheus historia recounts the lives of Syrian ascetics and presents their intercession and discipline as models of true worship.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Seleucia ad Calycadnum in Isauria
authors.sig: Metropolitan of Seleucia in Isauria. He opposed Eutyches at the Synod of Constantinople in 448 but wavered at Ephesus in 449 before signing Leo's Tome in 450. He wrote 41 sermons, mostly exegetical and hortatory. He also wrote two books on the life and miracles of St. Thecla, which argue that miracles confirm the preaching of faith.
His Euthalian Sections spread through the whole Greek Church and remain a dating tool for New Testament manuscripts; the work here presents his divisions and prolegomena to Acts and the Epistles.

His two 'centuries' of capitative maxims — one practical, against demons and passions for beginners; one theological, for advanced readers — entered the Philokalia and remain a primary witness to early Byzantine monastic teaching on grace, repentance, and apatheia.

authors.aff: Empress consort of Theodosius II; later resident of Jerusalem
authors.sig: The Augusta who was consort of the emperor settled in Jerusalem, where she endowed churches. She wrote Homeric verse retelling biblical stories. A narrative under her name tells of Cyprian of Antioch's conversion from magic through the virgin Justina.

His dialogue Theophrastus is a Christian defense of the soul's immortality and the body's resurrection argued against Platonist objections, showing how a convert used Neoplatonic method while rejecting doctrines incompatible with Christian dogma.

Bishop of Mytilene on Lesbos and a lawyer in Constantinople. He studied rhetoric in Gaza and philosophy in Alexandria. His Discourse on the Creation of the World argues against the Platonist Ammonius, and his Disputation against Certain Writings of the Manichaeans opposes Manichaean writings.

authors.aff: son of a presbyter of Cyzicus, Bithynia
authors.sig: Son of a presbyter in Bithynia, he compiled the Acts of the First Council of Nicaea in three books around 475. He wrote them to show that the Nicene Fathers did not teach Monophysitism, drawing on Theodoret and Dalmatius. Recent study has restored its value as a witness to how the Council's acts were transmitted.
His gospel synopsis founded the section-numbering system behind the Eusebian canons, the earliest apparatus for reading the four Gospels in parallel.

Patriarch of Constantinople from 458 to 471, he presided over a council of eighty-one bishops whose letter condemns selling ordinations for money. The letter anathematizes those who ordain for payment and insists that the Spirit's grace cannot be bought.

authors.aff: Bishop of Asculum (as given by the title of the work held)
authors.sig: The single surviving piece is a compact Chalcedonian polemic: it argues for two natures in Christ united indivisibly, against Theopaschites and Eutychians/Miaphysites, with side references to Arius, Manichaeus, Valentinus, and Eutyches.

Metropolitan bishop of Bostra in Arabia by 457 and a pronounced opponent of Origen. His long refutation of the Apology for Origen survives only in fragments. A homily on the Nativity of John the Baptist is ascribed to him though its authorship is doubted.

Archimandrite and monk who led the monks of Constantinople to the imperial palace in 431 to demand a hearing for Cyril of Alexandria's case. A short historical text on a deposition is attributed to him and argues that departure from grace brings condemnation.
The surviving fragment preserves a Chalcedonian account of the two natures acting 'with each other's communion,' directed against both Apollinarian and Eutychian readings.

Bishop of Berytus, he was named in 448 to examine a bishop of Edessa for Nestorianism. He also attended the council of August 449. A Chalcedonian polemic against the Monophysites defends the two-natures formula, arguing that each nature works its own with communion of the other.

The pages held are the editorial prolegomena establishing what Cosmas wrote and when; his Christian Topography itself matters as an early Byzantine biblical cosmography with some of the oldest surviving world maps.

authors.aff: Advocate in the courts at Constantinople
authors.sig: An advocate in the courts at Constantinople and a secular historian and poet. His unfinished Histories in five books continue Procopius, and they defend written history as a providential aid that saves great deeds from oblivion and teaches virtue more gently than philosophy. He also wrote the Daphniaca, short love poems in epic meter.

authors.n: John the Faster, Patriarch of Constantinople
authors.sig: Patriarch of Constantinople from 582 until his death in 595, he took the contested title of ecumenical patriarch and drew Roman objection. His penitential canons argue that God wills repentance rather than the sinner's death, against those who impose heavy penances.

authors.aff: Abbot of St. Catherine's Monastery, Mount Sinai
authors.sig: His works form a seventh-century manual of dogma and controversy. Christology dominates, argued through Old Testament types read as prefiguring Christ's two natures, with sustained polemic against the Jews, Severus of Antioch, the Manichaeans and Nestorius.

Patriarch of Antioch who was deposed and exiled by Justin II in 570 for opposing the emperor's teaching on Christ's body. His works defend Chalcedonian Christology and argue that Christ's body was subject to corruption and that bishops must openly resist emperors on matters of faith.

authors.n: Anastasius, Abbot of St. Euthymius' Monastery
authors.aff: Abbot of the monastery of St. Euthymius, Palestine
authors.sig: Abbot of St. Euthymius in Palestine around 741. His writings held that adoration of creatures is honor rather than worship and that prayer is owed to God alone. John wrote against him in 749 over his reading of the Trisagion as referring to the Son alone.
His letter on the death of Maximus is a contemporary witness to the Confessor's final persecution and trial under Constans II, and a vehicle preserving fragments of Hippolytus.

authors.aff: Monk and abbot of the Laura of St. Sabas near Jerusalem
authors.sig: A Galatian by birth, he lived as a solitary before becoming abbot of the Laura of St. Sabas near Jerusalem. He witnessed the Persian capture of Jerusalem in 614 and the massacre of forty-four monks. His Pandect of the Holy Scripture gathers moral teaching from Scripture and earlier writers on humility and prayer.

authors.aff: Priest and abbot of a monastery in Libya
authors.sig: Priest and abbot of a monastery in Libya. His one surviving work is four centuries of aphorisms on love and self-control. The 400 acrostic chapters treat life according to the nous. Maximus the Confessor addressed several works to him.

A monk at Raithu on the Sinai Peninsula, he wrote in Greek around 600 and is counted the last of the Neo-Chalcedonian authors. His Preparation (Proparaskeue) reconciles the terminology of Cyril of Alexandria with the canons of Chalcedon against anti-Chalcedonian readings.

authors.aff: Presbyter of the church of Jerusalem
authors.sig: Priest of the church of Jerusalem and biblical interpreter in the early fifth century. Tradition credits him with annotating all of Scripture. His fragments on the Psalms and the prophets read the Law in a Christ-centered way against Jewish interpretation.

His two surviving saints' lives — John the Almsgiver and Symeon the Fool — are among the principal Byzantine hagiographies, presenting virtue as attainable and teachers as bound to embody their doctrine.

authors.aff: Monk and priest, Mar Saba monastery near Jerusalem
authors.sig: Monk and priest at Mar Saba near Jerusalem, he defended the veneration of icons against the iconoclast emperor Leo III. His Exposition of the Orthodox Faith systematized Greek dogmatic theology, and he wrote the Three Treatises on the Divine Images.

authors.aff: Monk and presbyter (or bishop) of Euboea
authors.sig: Monk and presbyter, or possibly bishop, of Euboea, placed between 601 and 799. He wrote a homily on the Conception of the Mother of God that argues from Isaiah, Psalm 45 and 1 Kings that Mary was immaculate.

Jurist of Antioch who later moved to Constantinople and wrote the Chronographia, a world chronicle in eighteen books from mythical history to the reign of Justinian I. He wrote in the popular Greek of lay and monastic readers, and the end of Book 18 is likely by a later Orthodox author.

Chalcedonian Bishop of Harran who wrote in Greek, Syriac and Arabic and was counted the first known Christian writer in Arabic. His Greek works argued for the Trinity, the incarnation, sin and baptism. He debated Monophysites at the court of Ashot Msakeri in Armenia.

Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 715 to 730, who resigned his see rather than accept the iconoclast decrees of Emperor Leo III the Isaurian. He was made a eunuch and sent to a monastery after his father's execution in 668. His work Saint Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople (PG 98) defends the veneration of images.

Sicilian bishop of Agrigento from about 590 and correspondent of Pope Gregory I. A commentary on Ecclesiastes is attributed to him, but scholars dispute that attribution and the biography that describes his career.

The single work here, printed in PG 98, is an exegetical treatise on how to read Scripture's anthropomorphic language about God: it distinguishes three species of Hebrew scriptural idioms, treats figurative attributions of body and passion to God, divine anger and regret as accommodation, notes that God does not literally learn by testing, and reads covenant imagery of marriage and sonship as figu

authors.aff: Deacon of the church of Catania, Sicily
authors.sig: Deacon of the church of Catania in Sicily. At the Second Council of Nicaea in 787 he spoke for Thomas, archbishop of Sardinia. His contribution defends Christ as the gate opened by scriptural interpretation, against heretics who block the way of faith.

The material printed under his name in PG 98 centers on the iconoclast controversy: it defends the aid of departed saints, rejects additions to scripture, denies the title of universal patriarch, and argues against the Iconoclasts, simoniacs, and Emperor Constantine VI.

authors.aff: Abbot of the Stoudios Monastery, Constantinople
authors.sig: Abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople and a chief opponent of iconoclasm. He wrote three refutations defending the veneration of images. His organization of the Studium became a model for monasteries on Mount Athos and in Russia.
His work is an early witness to Byzantine sacramental theology of confession and penance, written amid the first iconoclast controversy.

Byzantine monk who preached against Iconoclasm in Constantinople after Leo V deposed Patriarch Nikephoros in 815. A short polemic against Mahomet and the Saracens survives under his name. It argues that apostles could bind and loose sins and that the eucharist is truly Christ's body and blood.

The work here is an eight-page homiletic text on sin, Adam's fall, repentance, and the salvation of the thief by faith in Christ alone, together with a defense of its attribution to Christopher against Allatius.

Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 843, he restored the veneration of icons and ended the second Iconoclasm. Born in Syracuse Sicily, he was a monk and abbot before Empress Theodora chose him as patriarch. Sources differ on whether he died in 846 or 847.

authors.aff: Deacon and chartophylax of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople; later Bishop (archbishop) of Nicomedia
authors.sig: A deacon and chartophylax of Hagia Sophia who became Bishop of Nicomedia. Eight of his ten surviving homilies concern the Mother of God. His Good Friday homily on her lamentations is the first extant homily on the Crucifixion from a Marian viewpoint.

Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople in two periods, 858–867 and 877–886. His Syntagma and Nomocanon are the classic source of ancient church law for the Greek Church, comparable to Gratian in the West. Among his works is the Myriobiblon, a survey of books he had read.

Monk of Edessa and author of the Greek polemic Elenchus et Confutatio Agareni. The work answers Muslim objections to the Trinity, the Incarnation and confession. It argues from Muhammad's life that he was an impostor.

authors.aff: Monk (name David) at the monastery of Agathos, Constantinople
authors.sig: A Byzantine monk and lawyer who opposed the tetragamy of Leo VI and broke with his teacher Arethas of Caesarea over it. He wrote about fifty saints' lives. He also wrote a Psalms commentary with moral exhortation for each psalm and a Life of Patriarch Ignatios that attacks Photios.

authors.aff: Archimandrite of the Pege Monastery, Constantinople
authors.sig: Archimandrite of the Pege Monastery and a monk who supported Patriarch Ignatius of Constantinople. He was sent to Rome to represent Ignatius and is generally credited with the report to Pope Nicholas I on the Constantinopolitan situation.

Monk and hymnographer of Constantinople who defended icon veneration during the iconoclast persecution under Leo the Armenian. His Theotokia are verse theology affirming Mary as ever-virgin Mother of God. Some hymns under his name are uncertain, since he is often confused with an older Joseph of Thessalonica.

A Byzantine writer who flourished around 900 at Constantinople, esteemed there for learning and genius. His two works in PG 106 are exegetical and historical surveys of Scripture and doctrine that defend Mary as theotokos of the pre-existent Word.

authors.n: Andrew, Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia
authors.sig: His Apocalypse commentary is the oldest surviving Greek commentary on Revelation by a recognized Father, the source most later Eastern commentators drew on, and it fixed a distinct text type of Revelation known as the Andreas type.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Caesarea Mazaca in Cappadocia
authors.sig: His Apocalypse commentary is the oldest extant Greek scholia on Revelation, drawing on Andrew of Caesarea, and reads the beast as Mohammed while arguing for a pre-destruction date of the book.

The PG 106 volume here holds his verse paraphrases of the biblical canticles and Marian sermons (including an Annunciation sermon and probably a Panteleemon encomium), arguing theses such as 'God became man that man might become god' and that joy through Mary reverses Eve's curse.

Lay homilist and imperial wardrobe officer in Constantinople, active in the late eighth or early ninth century. He wrote five sermons on the translation of John Chrysostom's relics and three encomia for Zechariah. His four Dormition homilies survive only in an early Latin translation.

authors.aff: magistros and envoy at the court of Constantinople
authors.sig: Byzantine official who served as envoy to Bulgaria and the Abbasid Caliphate under Leo VI. He wrote poems, letters and an epitome of interpretation of the Old and New Testament. His scholia on Genesis argue that the spirit over the waters is air rather than the Holy Spirit.

Byzantine emperor from 886 to 912, called the Wise or the Philosopher. He wrote the Compendious Selection of Laws of Leo and Constantine and the Novel Constitutions, which became the legal code of the Byzantine Empire. He also wrote the Tactics on military affairs and theological and oracular works.

authors.aff: Abbot (igumen) of the monastery he founded at Sygria (Sigriane), Bithynia
authors.sig: Abbot of the monastery at Sygria and a confessor who was imprisoned for opposing Iconoclasm under Leo V. His Chronographia is a source for seventh- and eighth-century Byzantine history. The volume PG 108 is largely hagiographic and encomiastic in character and presents him as sanctified from the womb.
His Chronicle is one of the continuations of Theophanes and a principal source for Byzantine imperial history between Theophanes's stopping point and his own time.

authors.aff: Librarian of the Roman Church under Adrian II
authors.sig: Librarian of the Roman Church under Adrian II and the most learned Greek scholar of ninth-century Rome. He translated Greek conciliar texts into Latin, defending image-veneration with the principle that honor paid to an image passes to its prototype. His History of the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs ties the true church to episcopal succession.

authors.aff: Priest of the imperial palace at Thessalonica
authors.sig: His Account of the Sack of Thessalonica is the primary eyewitness narrative of the 904 sack, reading the calamity as divine judgment for the city's sins and crediting its martyr-saint with delivering it.

authors.aff: Monk in Constantinople under Michael III
authors.sig: A monk in Constantinople under Michael III who wrote a four-book Chronicle from the Creation to 842. He aimed only at what was useful and necessary, told with strict adherence to truth. The work is fiercely anti-iconoclast and full of patristic quotation.

authors.n: Nicholas I Mystikos, Patriarch of Constantinople
authors.sig: Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 901 to 907 and again from 912 to 925. His letters from the tetragamy controversy and the Bulgarian war argue over patriarchal authority and the excommunication of an emperor.
His life of Gregory of Nazianzus is one of the surviving early accounts of that father, and the text here shows how a later Greek writer read Constantine and the Arian controversy.
His work here is a polemic against Baronius on the marks of the true church and the authority of episcopal succession.

authors.aff: Bishop of Beth Raman (north of Tagrit/Tikrit), under the see of Antioch
authors.sig: Bishop of Beth Raman under the see of Antioch, who wrote a Commentary on Paradise arguing for two senses of the garden. He taught that paradise was both a real corporeal garden of trees and river and an incorporeal state of the contemplative virtuous life. Andreas Masius translated it into Latin in 1569.

authors.aff: Imperial secretary and Eparch of Constantinople under Romanos I, Constantine VII, Romanos II
authors.sig: Imperial secretary and Eparch of Constantinople under Romanos I, Constantine VII, and Romanos II. He retired when Nikephoros II Phokas took power in 963. A brief surviving text from PG 111 treats original sin and mortality. It argues against Julian the Apostate.
His work here is the hagiographic Life of Symeon Salos, treating prayer, demons, virtues, sin, and last things through a mix of narrative, exegesis, and moral instruction.

Melkite Patriarch of Alexandria from 933 until his death in 940. He practiced medicine and knew no Greek, working from Syriac translations. His world chronicle Nazm al-Jawhar runs from Adam to 938. It is a major source for the history of Egypt, Syria and Palestine under Persian occupation and early Islam.

authors.aff: Byzantine emperor (Macedonian dynasty), reigned 6 June 913 – 9 November 959
authors.sig: Byzantine emperor of the Macedonian dynasty who reigned from 913 to 959 but ruled alone only from 945. He commissioned or compiled works on court ceremony, imperial administration, and provincial geography. Among his works, the Book of Ceremonies and De Administrando Imperio are primary sources for these subjects.
His held work is a record of penitential preaching directed at converts and dissenters, notable for its pastoral method of adapting exhortation to hearers.

His epic on the capture of Crete helped establish the twelve-syllable line as the standard metre of middle and later Byzantine verse, and the material printed under his name in PG 113 reads Byzantine history as evidence of divine judgment on the proud and the peace-breaking.

His ten-volume menologion — the revised lives of the saints arranged by feast day that fill these volumes of Migne — was labelled 'a revolution in the field of hagiography' by Albert Ehrhard and made him the principal compiler of the saints' legends in the Menologia of the Byzantine Church.

authors.aff: Head of the philosophy faculty, imperial university of Constantinople (appointed by Constantine IX in 1045)
authors.sig: His advocacy of Platonic philosophy as integrable with Christian doctrine renewed Byzantine classical learning and later influenced the Italian Renaissance.

His constitutions show a pious emperor legislating directly on ecclesiastical property, protection of the poor, and civil law, making them primary evidence for Byzantine imperial theology and legal practice around 1000.

authors.aff: Deacon in the imperial palace, Constantinople
authors.sig: For the reigns of Nicephorus II Phocas and John Tzimiskes he is the only contemporary historian, making his history the primary narrative source for Byzantine wars against the Arabs, the conquest of Antioch, and the campaigns against Sviatoslav of Kiev.

Byzantine emperor from 963 to 969, born in Cappadocia to a military family. He retook Crete and completed the conquest of Cilicia before he was murdered in 969. A military treatise on skirmishing survives under his name.

Byzantine author known only through fragments of his Chronicle, mostly concerning the Holy Family. The sources disagree on his date, placing him between about 650 and 750 or in the tenth or eleventh century.

authors.aff: Deacon and skeuophylax of Hagia Sophia; later metropolitan of Nicaea
authors.sig: Deacon and skeuophylax of Hagia Sophia who later served as metropolitan of Nicaea and wrote saints' lives of Tarasios and Nikephoros. His exegetical fragments on Genesis explain Eve's formation from Adam's side and the devil's envy-driven temptation.

authors.aff: Monk and abbot at Mount Sinai
authors.sig: Monk and abbot at Mount Sinai who wrote ascetical and exegetical works on prayer and the avoidance of oaths. He was a disciple and defender of John Chrysostom. His writings treat virtuous life as the way to the heavenly inheritance.

The work preserved here is a brief exegetical and polemical text arguing from Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, David, Daniel, Abraham, and Gideon that the Old Testament witnesses to the Trinity and that true Israel is inward faith rather than descent.

Compiler of the Suda, a Greek encyclopedic lexicon of about 30,000 entries. Nothing certain is known of him beyond what the lexicon shows. It draws on earlier authors and preserves quotations from ancient writers whose works are otherwise lost.

A bishop of Trikka in Thessaly is credited with commentaries on Acts, the Catholic Epistles and the Pauline Epistles. Manuscripts show the Acts and Catholic Epistle texts match those of Theophylact of Achrida. Its Apocalypse commentary is dated about 990 in one manuscript and is largely a modified version of Andrew of Caesarea's work.

authors.aff: Reputed bishop of Trikka (Trikala) in Thessaly
authors.sig: Reputed bishop of Trikka in Thessaly and the name attached to Greek New Testament commentaries not all by one author. His Commentary on the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians, Commentary on the Epistle to Titus and Commentary on the Epistle to Philemon draw on Andrew of Caesarea and were used in turn by Theophylact.

A monk and priest at the Kallistratos monastery in Constantinople. He wrote extant lives of the Virgin Mary and of Andrew the Apostle. He also published the first Greek guidebook of Jerusalem for pilgrims, which circulated in an Old Church Slavonic translation.

A monk of the Stoudites who became ecumenical patriarch of Constantinople in 1025, appointed by Emperor Basil II on his deathbed. He held the see until c. 1043 and issued numerous edicts, synods and disciplinary laws. His surviving works (PG 120) treat grace, prayer, the Holy Spirit and baptism.

authors.aff: Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Mamas in Xerocercus/Xylocercus, Constantinople
authors.sig: The first Eastern Christian mystic to write openly of his own visions of God. He taught that direct experience of God is available now. His works center on sanctification, grace, prayer and participation in the Holy Spirit.

Served as chartophylax (record-keeper) at Nicaea. His treatise De Schismate inter Ecclesiam Graecam et Romanam survives in manuscript and defends Constantinople against Rome. It argues that popes consented to the fifth and seventh synods and that sixth-synod canons against Rome were never received.

Bishop of Gaza, known from one dialogue with a Muslim interlocutor. The work defends the real presence of Christ in the sacrament against objections. Some catalogues list it under Pseudo-Samonas. The attribution to him is uncertain.

Archbishop of Ohrid from 1037 until his death in 1056, and earlier chartophylax at Hagia Sophia. His letters on azymes argue that Christ's priesthood after Melchizedek replaced the Mosaic passover, so unleavened bread belongs to the abolished law.

authors.aff: Monastery of Stoudios, Constantinople (probably hegoumenos at the end of his life)
authors.sig: A Byzantine monk who became a close disciple of Symeon the New Theologian, whose biography he wrote. He defended Symeon's teaching on contemplative prayer and wrote on sanctification, tears and prayer. He also wrote against Latin use of unleavened bread.
A leading figure of eleventh-century Constantinopolitan scholarship and hymnography, he stands at the center of the Psellos circle that shaped Byzantine intellectual life under Monomachos.

Deacon and orator of the Great Church at Constantinople toward the end of the ninth century. He wrote a life of Joseph the Hymnographer. His treatise Quid est consilium Dei in prima hominis formatione treats creation and the fall. It also treats original corruption transmitted from Adam and the Trinity as once hidden from idol-prone peoples.

authors.aff: Byzantine court official (proedrus); possibly a monk
authors.sig: A Byzantine court official called proedrus who compiled the Synopsis historion, a world chronicle from creation to 1057. After 811 much of it repeats another chronicler word for word. Its account of the Theopaschite controversy reports Chalcedonian defenders persecuted while orthodox laity resisted changes to the Trisagion.

His running commentary on nearly the whole New Testament — Gospels, Acts, Catholic Epistles, Pauline Epistles, Hebrews, and the Prophets represented here by Hosea — became one of the standard Byzantine exegetical texts, treasured in Orthodox tradition.

authors.aff: Caesar and panhypersebastos at the court of Alexios I Komnenos
authors.sig: General and statesman under Alexios I Komnenos, who held the titles Caesar and panhypersebastos and married Anna Komnene. He defended Constantinople against Godfrey of Bouillon in 1097 and wrote a history of the Komnenoi's rise to power.

authors.n: Nicholas III Grammaticus, Patriarch of Constantinople
authors.sig: Patriarch of Constantinople in the Byzantine tradition. Works printed under his name in PG 127 are attributed to him, but no external sources were found to confirm his career.

authors.aff: Monastery of the Black Mountain (Montagne Noire) near Antioch
authors.sig: A Byzantine monk who had first served as a soldier. He compiled a compendium of Scripture, canons and civil law around 1060 so that orthodox teaching would survive Saracen invasion. His works in PG 127 treat tribulation as refining fire and baptism as a bridal garment.

authors.aff: Deacon of St. Sophia, Constantinople; later Metropolitan of Heraclea in Pontus
authors.sig: Deacon of St. Sophia in Constantinople and later Metropolitan of Heraclea, he wrote a Commentary on the Orations of St. Gregory of Nazianzus (38–44). It defends the divinity of Christ and the Spirit against opponents and argues that God is known through his effects rather than his essence.

His homilies on the feasts of the Virgin are a major twelfth-century witness to Byzantine Marian doctrine — including an asserted immaculate conception of Mary — and the Vatican copy of them has been called 'the longest visual biography of the Virgin ever produced in Byzantium.'
Byzantine monk who wrote the Dioptra under Alexius I Comnenus. It is a five-book work in political verse, framed as a dialogue between soul and body and addressed to the monk Callinicus.

The pieces here are short Greek fragments on Christology, baptism, and the Spirit — including the ox and ass as Jews and Gentiles and the Spirit as pledge of adoption in baptism — directed against Manichaean, Arian, and Macedonian teaching.

Archbishop of Milan from 1101 or 1102 until a council deposed him around 1111 or 1112. While in Constantinople he delivered an oration to the emperor defending the filioque, and replies followed from others.

Byzantine empress who ruled as guardian for her son and later alone. She summoned the council that restored icons. A doctrinal work surviving under her name defends Mary's perpetual virginity and argues that God created man from nothing.

Presbyter in the Byzantine church whose Didactic Anthologion gathers ascetic chapters on sanctification, prayer and virtue. He argues that word and practice are mutually necessary. The work was long attributed to Maximus the Confessor and others before it was assigned to him.
The single work held is a synodal decree on marriage law, valuable as evidence of how church and emperor cooperated in enforcing canon law on matrimony.

A Byzantine writer whose works include De Paschate and a commentary on the Song of Songs. A short text under his name argues that synodal authority governs marriages and that the emperor must guard synodal decrees. Biblissima places him in the tenth to eleventh century.

authors.aff: Monastery of the Virgin Mary near Constantinople
authors.sig: Monk of the convent of the Virgin Mary near Constantinople, commissioned by Emperor Alexius I Comnenus to write the Panoplia Dogmatica against heretics. The work refutes heresy from the apostles to the Bogomils, and its Bogomil entry remains the chief source on that sect.

Eldest daughter of Emperor Alexius I Comnenus. She wrote the Alexiad in fifteen books, finished by 1148. It covers her father's reign from 1069 to his death in 1118 and is the chief source for that reign.

authors.aff: Deacon of Hagia Sophia, patriarchal notary, protoproedros of the protosynkelloi, and nomophylax in Constanti
authors.sig: Byzantine monk who had served as deacon of Hagia Sophia and patriarchal notary in Constantinople. He was at the court of Roger II in Palermo, where he wrote a treatise on the five patriarchates. The work argues from an Eastern, anti-Roman standpoint and was controversial in the West.

authors.aff: Author printed in Migne PG 132 under the name 'John of Antioch'; further identification uncertain
authors.sig: The fragments preserve material drawn from lost earlier historians (via the excerptors and Suidas) and are mined here chiefly for their narrative of Roman imperial history rather than for original theology.

authors.n: Isaac the Great, Catholicos of Armenia
authors.sig: Patriarch of the Armenian Church from about 387 until his death around 438–439, he led it after Armenia was partitioned between Byzantium and Persia. With Mesrop Mashtots he supported the invention of the Armenian alphabet. A doctrinal work under his name (PG 132) may not be his.

authors.aff: Oikonomos and nomophylax of the Great Church, Constantinople
authors.sig: His scholia on the canons are a standard Byzantine reference for how twelfth-century Constantinople read marriage law, ordination discipline, and penitential rules.

authors.aff: Imperial secretary (grammatikos) to Emperor Manuel I Komnenos
authors.sig: Imperial secretary to Manuel I Komnenos and author of a history covering 1118 to 1176. His work continues Anna Komnene's Alexiad through the reigns of John II and Manuel I, ending abruptly at Myriokephalon. He writes in a plain style modeled on Xenophon and as a partisan of Byzantine supremacy over Western powers.

authors.aff: Court poet, Constantinople; monk late in life
authors.sig: Court poet at Constantinople under John II and Manuel I Komnenos, he wrote occasional verse and prose for many patrons. His Epitaph for Theodora and Epithalamium argue that virtue comes through the will rather than lineage, and that philosophy aims at practice rather than knowledge.

authors.aff: Court official under Alexios I Komnenos; later monk on Hagia Glykeria
authors.sig: Byzantine historian and canonist who served Alexios I Komnenos as head justice and private secretary. After retiring to a monastery on Hagia Glykeria he wrote his Historical Epitome, which runs from creation to 1118 and preserves lost books of Cassius Dio.

authors.aff: Court official under Alexios I Komnenos; later monk on Hagia Glykeria
authors.sig: A Byzantine historian and canonist who held high office under Alexios I Komnenos before retiring to Hagia Glykeria around 1118. There he wrote his Historical Epitome, a universal chronicle from creation to 1118 drawing on lost books of Cassius Dio.

authors.aff: Recluse in a cave hermitage above Paphos, Cyprus
authors.sig: Cypriot Orthodox recluse who lived in a cave hermitage above Paphos from 1159. A three-page work in PG 135 argues that calamities are God's just judgment for sin and that affliction leads sinners to forgiveness.

Metropolitan of Ephesus, with dates uncertain and ca. 1195 given in one source. He wrote on the procession of the Spirit to imperial recipients and against the schismatic Arsenites. He argues that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and rejects the Filioque.

Bishop of Methone in Messenia, he advised Emperor Manuel I Komnenos and debated the Latins on the filioque. His survey argues that the fathers understood procession as existence and that reunion with the Latins requires renouncing the filioque. Modern scholarship regards his Refutation of Proclus as his greatest work.

Archbishop of Thessalonica and teacher of rhetoric in the Patriarchal school. He negotiated with the Norman invaders during the sack of 1185 and wrote On the Capture of Thessalonica by the Latins. His works rebuke hypocritical monks and urge obedience to magistrates.

A Greek monk of the eleventh century, about whom nothing else is recorded. His Loci Communes (Commonplaces) gathers moral sentences from Scripture, the Fathers and earlier Jewish and pagan writers. Its maxims insist that teaching be confirmed by works and that true fasting means abstaining from sins rather than from foods.

authors.aff: Titular Patriarch of Antioch, resident in Constantinople
authors.sig: His Scholia on the Nomocanon preserved knowledge of many otherwise unknown Byzantine legal and theological source documents and remains a standard authority on Eastern Orthodox canon law.

authors.aff: Metropolitan of Kiev and all Rus'
authors.sig: Metropolitan of Kiev who supported union with Rome and proclaimed that union in 1452. His Homily on the Virgin Mary argues from fittingness that all things existed for her sake and that God became incarnate because no creature sufficed for man's restoration.
The work here is a Byzantine anti-Filioque dialogue that stages the Greek-Latin dispute over the Spirit's procession as a formal exchange of objections, responses, and proofs.

authors.aff: Logothetes ton sekreton under the Angelos emperors, Constantinople
authors.sig: Civil official under the Angelus emperors who witnessed the sack of Constantinople in 1204. He wrote a History of the years 1118 to 1207 and a Treasury of Orthodox Faith. The Treasury gathers polemic against Arians, Eunomians, Nestorians and Latins.

Metropolitan of Athens from about 1182, he defended the Acropolis against Leo Sgouros and surrendered it to Boniface of Montferrat's Crusaders in 1205. His homilies and orations preach on Christ's descent, the harrowing of hell, and the resurrection, and they attack Leo Sgouros.

Byzantine bishop of Alania to whom Biblissima attributes several Greek texts. A short Greek work in PG 140 argues that the Spirit gathers distant brethren into one assembly and that God turns the malice of the wicked to good.

His single surviving work is a late Byzantine mystagogical exposition of the liturgy as a symbol of the whole economy of salvation, useful for sacramental theology and for evidence of anti-Bogomil polemic in Asia Minor.
A scholar-emperor whose surviving theological pieces defend the Greek doctrine of the Spirit's procession and an apophatic-affirmative account of the divine names against Latin teaching.

A Byzantine monk who wrote a short polemic on whether orders given by heretics or uncanonically installed bishops are valid. The work defends Theodore the Studite as having died in communion with the patriarchs and opposes Emperor Michael VIII Palaeologus and Arsenius. It asserts that schism is the worst evil in the church.

authors.aff: Chief minister (mesazōn) to Andronikos II Palaiologos
authors.sig: Mesazōn to Andronikos II Palaiologos and later governor of Thessalonica, he was a rival of Theodore Metochites. He wrote a polemical treatise against Plato and Plotinus denying the pre-existence and transmigration of souls.

Pope from 1254 to 1261 who continued Innocent's war against Manfred and gave Sicily to Edmund, son of Henry III of England. He supported the mendicant orders and canonized Clare of Assisi in 1255. A polemical history asserting the supreme authority of the Roman see over a Greek church survives under his name.

Franciscan friar and Minister General of his order before he became pope in 1471. He founded the Vatican Library and built the Sistine Chapel. He authorized the Spanish Inquisition in 1478 by the bull Exigit Sinceræ Devotionis.

authors.aff: Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, 2 June 1275 – 26 December 1282
authors.sig: Patriarch of Constantinople from 1275 to 1282 and the chief Greek advocate of reunion with Rome. He wrote on the procession of the Holy Spirit and argued that the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son.

authors.n: George Metochites, Deacon of the Great Church
authors.sig: Archdeacon of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople and a fervent supporter of the union of Greek and Latin Churches agreed in 1274. A tract on the Spirit's procession from the Father through the Son survives under his name. After the union ended, he was charged with heresy and spent about forty-five years in prison or exile.

His iambic world chronicle is a compact Byzantine verse history of thirteen centuries, known only through a single Vatican manuscript, and the edition here also carries polemic against iconoclast emperors and the Latins.

authors.aff: High official under Andronikos II Palaiologos
authors.sig: Byzantine statesman and scholar who rose through imperial offices to serve as personal adviser from about 1305 to 1328. In a prolegomenon on theological method he argues that 'from the son' expresses relation rather than principal cause. He traces a shared harsh Greek style to Egyptian schooling in Philo, Ptolemy and Clement.

authors.aff: Hieromonk of a monastery in Thessalonica
authors.sig: The Syntagma is a major late Byzantine synthesis of canon with civil law, and its alphabetic arrangement made it widely transmitted in the Orthodox Slavic world.

authors.n: Theodulus the Monk or Thomas Magister
authors.aff: Court of Andronikos II Palaiologos; later monk at Thessalonica
authors.sig: Byzantine grammarian and confidential adviser at the imperial court before he took monastic vows at Thessalonica. He taught Philotheus Coccinus and Gregory Acindynus and wrote an encomium on Gregory Nazianzen arguing that praising the saints is a duty.

A priest at Hagia Sophia in Constantinople who taught rhetoric and theology. His Ecclesiastica Historia was planned in 23 books, and only the first eighteen are known. It is a major source on early Christian doctrinal disputes, including polemic against Marcion and Origen.

His Church History is a major documentary source for early Christianity's doctrinal controversies — above all Arianism — and for hagiographical and liturgical material, even where it reworks Eusebius and earlier historians.

His treatise 'On Watchfulness and the Guarding of the Heart' teaches nepsis (watchfulness) through a method of gathering the mind into the heart with controlled breathing while praying, laying groundwork for later hesychast practice.

The PG 147 volume here holds works attributed to him — orations on Peter and Paul and on the burial of Christ that scholarship reassigns from Gregory of Nazianzus to Planudes, plus his recension of the Greek Anthology into seven books with lemmata to the epigrams.

authors.aff: Chartophylax (keeper of the archives) at Constantinople under Andronicus II
authors.sig: Keeper of the archives at Constantinople under Andronicus II. He wrote a 37-volume Byzantine History that is a primary source for fourteenth-century Byzantium. He argued against Gregory Palamas and held that Palamism leads to atheism.

authors.aff: Metropolitan of Thessalonica (consecrated 1361), though he never took possession of the see
authors.sig: Consecrated metropolitan of Thessalonica in 1361 but never took possession of the see. His anti-Latin writings on the Schism and papal primacy argue that disputed faith matters belong to an ecumenical synod. These writings say early popes decided doctrine only in council with other bishops.

authors.n: Theodore Meliteniotes, Archdeacon of the Great Church
authors.aff: Didaskalos ton didaskalon, Patriarchal School of Constantinople
authors.sig: His held work is an ethical-exegetical discourse defending the eucharistic conversion against typological/symbolic readings and schismatics, while also arguing that late Greek authors write with elegance and that novelty does not imply inferiority.

Byzantine jurist and universal judge of Thessalonica. He wrote the Hexabiblos in 1344–45, a six-book thematic compilation of Byzantine law. It formed the basis of Greek civil law until the new Civil Code of 1946. His De haeresibus is a canonical survey of church order, sacraments, and heresies.

Metropolitan of Philadelphia in the fourteenth century, known for arranging patristic extracts under headings he called 'golden heads'. A text under his name (PG 150) sets out canonical rulings on marriage and widowhood, and on pious practices such as women dressing as men and cutting their hair.

authors.aff: Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, February 1334 – 2 February 1347
authors.sig: He matters chiefly as the patriarchal leader of the anti-hesychast opposition to Gregory Palamas; the work here is a brief ascension homily transmitted under his name, engaged with Jacob Gretser's attribution of it to Philotheus.

Archbishop of Nicaea whose one surviving work is a dogmatic treatise against the Palamites and against deniers of real divine attributes. It covers sin, Christology, grace, the sacraments and last things. No source gives his birth or death dates.

authors.aff: Priest at the Mangana Monastery, Constantinople
authors.sig: Priest at the Mangana Monastery in Constantinople and adviser to Emperor John VI Cantacuzenus. He supported Gregory Palamas in the Hesychast controversy and is remembered for Life in Christ and the Commentary on the Divine Liturgy. Those two treatises teach union with Christ through baptism, chrismation and the Eucharist.

authors.aff: Eastern Orthodox Church, Mount Athos, Archbishopric of Thessalonica
authors.sig: A Doctor of the Eastern Orthodox Church. His defense of Hesychasm and of the distinction between essence and energies shaped late Byzantine and modern Orthodox dogmatics.

authors.n: John VI Kantakouzenos, Emperor of Constantinople
authors.aff: Byzantine emperor (r. 8 February 1347 – 10 December 1354); later monk as Joasaph Christodoulos
authors.sig: Byzantine emperor from 1347 to 1354 who later took monastic vows as Joasaph Christodoulos. He wrote a four-book History of his own times and four orations against Mohammed, arguing that the Alcoran is not the law of God. He called and presided at the Third Palamite Council of 1351.

A Byzantine monk and theologian born at Prilep, he was first a pupil of Gregory Palamas. From 1341 he denounced the teaching of Gregory Palamas on the Uncreated Light as Messalianism. He was excommunicated in 1347 and died in exile, apparently of the plague of 1348.

A Byzantine theologian of Constantinople who sided with the opponents of Gregory Palamas by 1342 at the latest. He wrote Palamiticarum Transgressionum Libri IV, which argues that God's essence is incomprehensible to creatures and that will and substance are distinct in God.

authors.aff: Mesazon (imperial chancellor) under three Byzantine emperors
authors.sig: His own works in this volume are chiefly anti-Islamic polemics and deliberative orations—arguments that the Alcoran is not the law of God and appeals against surrendering Gallipoli—written in service of his Latin-union, anti-Ottoman program. However, much of the volume's 630 pages consists of works by other authors (e.g., John Cantacuzenus's apologies, a translation of Brother Richard's treatise),

authors.aff: Order of Preachers; missionary in Baghdad

authors.sig: A Greek monk active around 1400 who defended Latin teaching on the procession of the Holy Spirit. In De processione Spiritus Sancti he defends the Filioque against those who say the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, and he argues that hatred of the Latins drives that rejection.

Archbishop of Thessalonica from 1416 or 1417, he saw the city pass to Venetian rule as Ottoman forces closed in. He wrote on prayer, ordination and the sacraments. He also wrote against the Latins, Barlaam, and Nestorius.

authors.aff: Byzantine diplomat and scholar; ambassador to Italy; teacher of Greek at Florence
authors.sig: Byzantine diplomat and scholar who led an embassy to Venice in 1390 to seek aid. He taught Greek at Florence and translated Homer, Aristotle and Plato into Latin. His letter comparing old and new Rome argues that the city's monuments are surer witnesses than written histories.

His account of the 1422 siege is a vivid eyewitness narrative combining military history with religious polemic against the Turks and their emir Mersaita, and it defends Constantinople's standing as Rome's equal rather than its colony.

Byzantine emperor who ruled alone from 1391 until his death in 1425, and whose diplomacy delayed the conquest by the Turks for some fifty years. He wrote ethical and political orations, morning prayers and dialogues against Islam and the Turks. He argued that free will rather than nature makes men good or bad.
His Account of the Last Capture of Thessalonica is a primary eyewitness narrative of the Ottoman conquest of 1430, reading the calamity as divine punishment for sin.
Courtier to Constantine XI and an eyewitness to the fall of Constantinople in 1453. His chronicle covers 1413 to 1477 and reads events through providence, sin, and divine judgment.

authors.aff: Imperial secretary (grammatikos) under Manuel I Komnenos; later monk in Constantinople
authors.sig: Imperial secretary to Manuel I and later a monk in Constantinople. He was accused of magic and condemned to blinding around 1159. His Chronicle runs from Creation to 1118 and mixes theology with antiquarian curiosities.

A Byzantine writer whose surviving tract argues against the Latin teaching on the procession of the Holy Spirit. It opposes Argyropulos, holding that procession from the will would make the Spirit a creature. Whether this tract is by the eleventh-century John the Deacon is not established.

Author of a short Greek polemic answering John Argyropoulos on the procession of the Holy Spirit. It argues that the Father alone is the cause and principle of the Son and the Spirit. It reads the priority of the persons as an order of procession rather than of time.

Byzantine author of a Greek polemic against the Latins on the Filioque, answering objections and citing Gregory the Theologian and Athanasius. He argues that the Father alone is cause of the Spirit and rejects the Council of Florence on this point.

authors.aff: Teacher of Greek and Aristotelian philosophy at Florence and later Rome
authors.sig: A leading émigré Byzantine humanist who carried Greek learning into fifteenth-century Italy, he appears in this volume chiefly as the target of anti-Latin trinitarian polemic over the procession of the Spirit.

authors.aff: Patriarchate of Constantinople (hieromnemon, dikaiophylax, megas chartophylax, megas oikonomos)
authors.sig: Byzantine cleric and scholar who held several offices at the Patriarchate of Constantinople and was a close collaborator of Gennadios Scholarios. He wrote the Refutatio Argyropuli, an anti-unionist reply to John Argyropoulos that defends the Spirit's procession from the Father alone.
The single held volume is a historical account apparently of the 1453 Ottoman siege attributed to his name, not a theological work by the patriarch.
His single surviving work here is a Greek polemic against Islam and Turkish rule, useful for how Byzantine-era writers framed Muslim doctrine and conquest as heresy and chastisement.

A Byzantine author wrote a brief Greek tract on the Trinity, the divine persons and the procession of the Spirit that argues against Latin theology on the Filioque. He is not the Venetian nobleman of the same name who kept a diary of the 1453 Ottoman siege of Constantinople.

authors.n: Gregory III Mammas, Patriarch of Constantinople
authors.sig: Ecumenical Patriarch who signed the 1439 union with Rome at Ferrara-Florence. He was forced out of Constantinople in 1450 and died in 1459 without recovering his throne. His writings defend the Greek doctrine that the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son against Latin teaching.

authors.aff: Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople (1454–1464/65), first under Ottoman rule
authors.sig: Served as an imperial judge and lay preacher at the court of John VIII Palaeologus and as a theological consultant at the Council of Florence.
