Trained in Latin scholastic theology and a devoted Aristotelian, he opposed the Union with Rome after Florence. He was Patriarch of Constantinople from 1454 to 1464/65, first under Ottoman rule.

authors.aff: Metropolitan of Ephesus, Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
authors.sig: He is revered in Eastern Orthodoxy as a 'Pillar of Orthodoxy' for successfully rallying resistance against the Council of Florence's union with the Roman Catholic Church.

The works catalogued under this name are almost certainly misattributed: they are Greek-father addenda defending papal primacy and church union, written after Nicholas V's death, while the historical pope is remembered chiefly for founding the Vatican Library rather than for theological writing.

authors.aff: Archbishop of Nicaea; later cardinal; titular Latin Patriarch of Constantinople
authors.sig: Archbishop of Nicaea who accepted the Union of Florence and became a cardinal. His treatise On the Procession of the Holy Spirit defends the Latin position on that doctrine. He became a monk in 1423 and studied under Gemistus Pletho at Mystras.

authors.aff: Professor at the restored University of Rome under Eugenius IV; translator and secretary for Pope Nicholas V
authors.sig: Taught Greek in Italy and translated Greek works for Pope Nicholas V, though his quarrelsomeness brought him conflicts with other scholars. His treatises On the Procession of the Holy Spirit defend the Latin Filioque against the Greeks, arguing that the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son and even from the Son as from the Father.

authors.aff: teacher of Greek literature in Bologna, Rome, Florence, Paris and London
authors.sig: The single work held is a philological note untangling which Andronicus appears in Renaissance sources, useful to readers tracking how the Byzantine teacher was confused with namesakes.
His handbook on receiving heretics is a primary witness to Byzantine admission practice; Theodore the Studite later used the same three-category scheme.

authors.aff: Scythian monk community at Constantinople (per work titles and correspondence with Pope Hormisdas)
authors.sig: His letters and professions preserve the Scythian monks' side of the Theopaschite controversy that shaped Chalcedonian Christology between the councils of Chalcedon and Constantinople II.

Bishop of Rome from 514 to 523, he ended the Acacian schism with Constantinople. Reunion was ratified in the cathedral of Constantinople on 28 March 519. His letters and decrees assert the apostolic see's authority over distant provinces.

Reader at Hagia Sophia who wrote two church histories. His Historia Tripartita joins the works of Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret into one account from Constantine to 439. His own continuation from 450 to 518 survives only in fragments.

Bishop of Scythopolis in the mid-sixth century. He had been tied to Origenism before he retracted. His treatise against Origenist errors argues that the movement repeats pagan and Manichaean error. It holds that penitent heretics should be received back into the Church.

Patriarch of Alexandria from 535 until his death in 566, he was a moderate Miaphysite who gained office through the support of Theodora. Justinian I summoned him to Constantinople. He spent the rest of his life there after refusing to accept Chalcedon. His dogmatic fragment argues for one nature of the incarnate Word.

Bishop of Emesa and a student of the Antiochene school, he declined the see of Alexandria in favor of Emesa. His homilies and orations treat Christology and Scripture, and they describe Christ's descent into hades.

The Disputation with Herbanus is a substantial surviving Greek anti-Jewish dialogue, arguing from Isaiah and the Psalms that Israel's remnant means those who believed in Christ; the Laws are a witness to Christian legislation attributed to a sixth-century Arabian kingdom.

Patriarch of Constantinople from 520 to 535 who ended the Acacian Schism with Pope Hormisdas. He accepted the decrees of Chalcedon and received back repentant Monophysite bishops. His anti-Monophysite polemic defends Chalcedonian Christology.

authors.aff: Bishop of Nineveh (consecrated c. 670, resigned after five months)
authors.sig: Consecrated bishop of Nineveh around 670, he resigned after five months and lived as an anchorite. His ascetic homilies on prayer, sanctification and the conquest of the passions became a fundamental source for Eastern and Western Christian mysticism.

authors.aff: Hermit near the monastery of Seridus, Gaza
authors.sig: A major Desert Father whose letters fixed the tradition of Gazan spiritual direction, represented here by polemical pieces against Origenist teaching on eternal punishment and the celestial orders.

Roman emperor from 527 to 565 and nephew of Justin I. He is remembered for the Corpus Juris Civilis and for building Hagia Sophia. He intervened directly in theology, and his edicts and treatise Against Origen attack the Origenists.

His Ekthesis (Admonitory Chapters) is an early and influential 'mirror for princes', teaching that the emperor is God's representative, that earthly kingship mirrors the heavenly kingdom, and that power from God obligates philanthropic action — themes central to Byzantine political theology.

A sixth-century Byzantine monk and Chalcedonian theologian who wrote Three Books against the Nestorians and Eutychians. He is credited with introducing Aristotelian logical categories into Christological theology.

Patriarch of Antioch from 527 until 545, he had earlier served as a military officer and civil administrator under Anastasius I and Justin I. He defended the Definition of Chalcedon against the Monophysites, and only fragments of his polemic survive.

authors.aff: Silentiary at the court of Justinian I, Constantinople
authors.sig: A Greek poet and courtier of Justinian I at Constantinople, and a silentiary who kept order in the Great Palace. His ecphrasis on Hagia Sophia describes Justinian's church and remains a primary witness to the building's original appearance.

The volume here presents him as orthodox on the resurrection, holding that soul and body are judged together after it, defending mixed chalice and consecration by prayer against Aquarians, and fixing Easter against Jewish Passover dating and Quartodeciman practice.

authors.aff: Advocate at Antioch; aide to Patriarch Gregory of Antioch
authors.sig: Advocate at Antioch and aide to Patriarch Gregory, he wrote a six-book Ecclesiastical History covering 431 to 594. It continues Eusebius after Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret and is a primary source for the Christological controversies of the fifth and sixth centuries.

Patriarch of Alexandria from about 580 until his death in 607 or 608. He combated Monophysitism and refuted the Novatians. His Palm Sunday oration and christological chapters survive through Photius. They argue that the divine nature remains impassible while the body suffers.

Patriarch of Jerusalem from 609 until his death in 632. He was carried into Persian captivity when the city fell in 614. A short work On the Holy Images survives under his name, defending veneration and arguing that honor shown to the image passes to its prototype.

Ascetic on Mount Sinai who became abbot of a monastery near Bethlehem and governed the see of Jerusalem as locum tenens after the city was sacked in 614. A treatise on Christology and the Trinity printed under his name cites writers later than his time, so it cannot be his work.
The work here is his Epiphany sermon on Isaiah 9:5, a Miaphysite defence of the title Theotokos and Mary's virginitas in partu, later used by anti-Chalcedonian writers.

authors.aff: Head of the rhetorical school of Gaza
authors.sig: Head of the rhetorical school of Gaza and a Christian sophist trained in Alexandria. He wrote Old Testament commentaries on Genesis, Exodus, Isaiah, Proverbs, and the Song of Songs. These preserve Hexaplar readings from Symmachus, Aquila, and Theodotion.

authors.aff: Monk of St. Theodosius Monastery near Jerusalem
authors.sig: His Spiritual Meadow is one of the earliest collections of hagiographical anecdote, recording the sayings, miracles, and ascetic practices of monks he met across the Middle East, and it became a model for medieval ascetic literature.
He is renowned for his theological defense of the two wills and energies of Christ against Monothelitism and for his liturgical and hagiographical writings.

His commentaries on Job and Ecclesiastes are notable Greek patristic treatments of those books, arguing that human actions proceed from free choice rather than fate or necessity and that no man is pure before God.

The single held epistle is an imperial letter on the Monothelite dispute, arguing that the five synods and approved fathers completed the faith, that faith must be persuaded rather than compelled, and that providence overrules human deliberation.

authors.aff: Mount Athos (Skete of Magoula near Philotheou); later monastery at Paroria, Bulgaria
authors.sig: A Byzantine monk who taught unceasing mental prayer as the common path for all monks and the teachable signs by which true grace is told from demonic deception. He lived on Mount Athos and founded a monastery at Paroria in Bulgaria. His disciple Patriarch Kallistos I wrote his life.

authors.n: Theodorus II Ducas Lascaris & Nicetas (Migne cols 1221-1395)
authors.sig: He stands out as one of the few Byzantine emperors who was also a prolific and competent theologian, composing substantial treatises on the procession of the Holy Spirit.

Patriarch of Constantinople from 712 to 715, chosen by the emperor for his Monothelite sympathies. He wrote a letter to Pope Constantine that defends the acts of the emperor's reign and asserts the headship of the apostolic see. The letter is set against writers who called him a Monothelite.

Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 806 to 815, when the iconoclast emperor Leo the Armenian deposed and exiled him. His writings against the Iconoclasts defend the veneration of images on the principle that honor paid to the image passes to its prototype. His argument also makes episcopal succession the mark of the true church.

authors.aff: Magistros and logothete at the Byzantine court
authors.sig: Byzantine historian and poet who held the court titles magistros and logothete. His world chronicle from Creation to 948 ends with an account of 842 to 948 that drew on his own recollections of 913 to 948 and defended the veneration of images as lawful and ancient against the iconoclasts.

The bishop of Antioch writes seven letters as he is taken to his death.
A philosopher turned Christian defends the faith to the emperor at Rome.

The greatest scholar of the early church settles at Caesarea in Palestine.
The Son is confessed one in being with the Father.
Gregory of Nazianzus presides for a time. The creed is completed.
John of Antioch becomes bishop of Constantinople.
Cyril of Alexandria against Nestorius: Mary is Theotokos.
He dies in exile for confessing two wills in Christ. Constantinople III vindicates him in 681.
The emperors move against the images. John of Damascus answers from Mar Saba.
The veneration of images is restored.
The most learned patriarch of Constantinople.
Athanasius the Athonite founds the Great Lavra.
The legates and Patriarch Michael Cerularius excommunicate each other.
A council at Constantinople confirms his teaching.
A union with Rome is proclaimed and soon rejected.
The city falls to Mehmed II.

Letters between the columns divide each one into quarters. PG 6:475B points to the second quarter of the left-hand column.
The Greek stands in one column and a Latin translation in the other. Each can be read against the other. Here the Latin is on the left.
Chapters are numbered in both columns. In the Latin an italic summary heads each one. Here Justin tells how he tried many philosophies before he settled with the Platonists.
Bold numbers in the text give the pages of the earlier edition Migne reprinted. With them older references can still be found.

q.A: καὶ σοῦ οὐκ ἔτι καὶ τοῦ καθέκαστα , ἐπεὶ οὐδ' ἂν ηὐχόμεθα αὐτῷ δι' ὅλης νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας. Τοῦτο δὲ ὅπῃ αὐτοῖς τελευτᾷ, οὐ χαλεπὸν συννοῆσαι. Ἄδεια γὰρ καὶ ἐλευθερία λέγειν καὶ ἕπεσθαι τοῖς δοξάζουσι ταῦτα, ποιεῖν τε ὅ τι βούλονται καὶ λέγειν, μήτε κόλασιν φοβουμένοις , μήτε ἀγαθὸν ἐλπίζουσί τι ἐκ Θεοῦ. For to those who hold these opinions, there is open an impunity and license to dispute and pursue whatever they please, and to do and say whatever they want, neither fearing any punishment, nor hoping for any good from God. For how should they fear or hope, who say that things will always be the same, and that you and I will live again in the same manner, having become neither better nor worse? Certain others, moreover, since they assume the soul to be immortal and incorporeal, think that they will not suffer punishment if they have done anything evil (for that which is incorporeal cannot suffer), nor do they any longer need anything from God, since the soul is immortal.
Then he, smiling politely, said: But what do you think about these matters, and what is your opinion about God, and what is your philosophy? Explain to us.
2. He relates that, having tasted of several philosophies, he finally attached himself to the Platonists.

I will indeed, I said, explain to you what seems right to me. For philosophy is truly the greatest possession and most precious before God, to whom it alone leads us and commends us; and truly holy are those who apply their minds to philosophy. But what philosophy is, and for what reason it was sent down to men, has escaped most people. For there would be neither Platonists, nor Stoics, nor Peripatetics, nor Theoretics, nor Pythagoreans, since this science is one. Why it has become many-headed, however, it is agreeable to state.
